These Page 4/30 findings suggest a strategic shift from blanket prevention to precision control, prioritizing active surveillance in densely populated urban fringes and areas undergoing infrastructure development. Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a natural focal disease caused by hantavirus infection, characterized primarily by acute onset, rapid disease progression, and a high mortality rate[1, 2]. China is one of the countries most severely affected by HFRS globally[3, 4]. Since the 1980s, the annual reported case count exceeded 100,000 for many years, placing a sustained and significant burden on the public health system[5, 6]. Although the national HFRS incidence rate in China has declined significantly in recent years following the implementation of comprehensive control measures—such as vaccination, reservoir host control, and health education—this trend does not indicate that epidemic risk has been eliminated, given the continued occurrence of sporadic cases and localized clusters[7, 8]. Notably, the epidemiological pattern of HFRS is not static but rather undergoes continuous evolution, driven by the interplay of natural environmental and socioeconomic factors[9, 10]. Particularly in the context of global warming, alterations in temperature and precipitation patterns can indirectly modulate hantavirus transmission risk by influencing the population dynamics and habitat distribution of reservoir hosts such as rodents[11, 12],thereby driving a geographical shift in high-risk areas[7, 10]. Against this backdrop, the epidemiological pattern of HFRS, traditionally predominant in northern regions, is currently exhibiting new characteristics of spatial variation[7, 9]. In recent years, the epidemiological dynamics of HFRS in Southwest China have attracted increasing attention due to rising incidence and the region's unique ecological landscape. While traditional high-incidence areas have long been concentrated in Northeast China and the North China Plain[13], Southwest China has recently exhibited an upward trend in reported cases and a gradual expansion of the endemic range, emerging as a potential high-risk region that warrants attention within the national prevention and control framework[14–16]. The study area is characterized by complex topography, featuring the coexistence of plateaus, mountains, and basins, diverse climatic types, and significant ecological heterogeneity; consequently, its natural conditions differ markedly from traditional HFRS-endemic areas[17]. This unique physiographical and climatic context may result in distinct reservoir species compositions, transmission pathways, and environmental drivers compared to the northern endemic areas, thereby shaping a region-specific pattern of HFRS transmission[18–20]. Previous studies have demonstrated that meteorological factors, socioeconomic factors, and land cover variables are closely associated with the occurrence of HFRS[21]. However, existing literature has largely concentrated on specific HFRS-endemic cities in southwestern China, with a primary emphasis on analyzing demographic characteristics and the spatiotemporal dynamics of the epidemic[19, 22–24]. Consequently, systematic and quantitative assessments regarding the distributional characteristics of HFRS risk factors and projected risk patterns at a holistic regional scale remain insufficient[7]. Given these limitations, it is imperative to conduct a comprehensive analysis of multidimensional influencing factors at a broader spatial scale. Therefore, this study aims to Page 5/30 systematically identify the combined effects of meteorological, socioeconomic, and land cover variables on the occurrence of HFRS in southwestern China, delineate potential disease risk zones, and quantify the population exposed to varying levels of risk, thereby providing a scientific basis for comprehensively assessing the associated public health burden and formulating region-specific prevention and control strategies. Methods HFRS surveillance data Surveillance data regarding HFRS cases in Southwest China spanning from 2014 to 2023 were sourced from the Infectious Disease Reporting System of the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (China CDC). All reported cases were confirmed strictly following the standardized diagnostic criteria formulated by the national CDC[25]. Base map and population data The base map was obtained from the National Platform for Common Geospatial Information Services (https://www.tianditu.gov.cn/; Map Approval No. GS(2024)0650), featuring polygon vector layers for provincial, prefectural, and county-level administrative divisions. Population data for southwestern China were derived from the Seventh National Population Census conducted in 2020, accessed via the National Bureau of Statistics of China (https://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/pcsj/rkpc/7rp/zk/indexce.htm). Population density was calculated by dividing the population size by the land area of each county. Environmental variables To investigate the environmental risk factors influencing the spatiotemporal distribution of HFRS in recent years, we collected data on a range of environmental variables, including meteorological factors and land cover. The selection of these variables was informed by prior studies and expert consultation regarding their potential impact on the spatiotemporal variation of the HFRS epidemic. Meteorological data for southwestern China spanning from 2014 to 2023 were obtained from the China Meteorological Data Service Centre (https://data.cma.cn/). The meteorological variables included in this study comprised the multi-year mean relative humidity, multi-year mean temperature, and multi-year mean precipitation. Using ArcGIS 10.8 software (ESRI, Redlands, CA, USA), raster layers representing the mean meteorological data for the 2014–2023 period were generated via the Kriging interpolation method. Elevation data were derived from a nationwide Digital Elevation Model (DEM) with a spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km, obtained from the National Earth System Science Data Center Page 6/30 (http://www.geodata.cn/data/datadetails.html?dataguid=201519481253546&docid=1301). Additionally, slope and aspect variables were calculated from the elevation data using ArcGIS 10.8 software. Land use data for the year 2013 were obtained from the National Earth System Science Data Center (https://www.geodata.cn/), provided as a raster layer with a spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km. Data for the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were obtained from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (https://www.tpdc.ac.cn/). As the most widely used vegetation index, NDVI indicates vegetation growth status and coverage, thereby comprehensively reflecting the environmental conditions of the region. All environmental variable datasets were projected to a unified geographic coordinate system and converted into raster format. Subsequently, the data were resampled to a consistent spatial resolution of 1 km and clipped to the extent of the study area using vector boundary data in ArcGIS 10.8. Study area Southwestern China is located between approximately 97°21′–110°11′ E and 21°08′–34°19′ N, situated at the eastern margin of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and encompassing the main body of the Yunnan- Guizhou Plateau. The region covers a total area of approximately 1.14 million km2 (Fig. 1). The region exhibits diverse climatic types, predominantly characterized by a subtropical monsoon climate alongside features of a plateau mountain climate. The mean annual temperature ranges from 8 to 20°C, with annual precipitation typically falling between 800 and 1800 mm. Notably, significant vertical climate differentiation is observed in local alpine valley areas[17]. According to the 2021 provincial statistical yearbooks and data from the Seventh National Population Census, the permanent resident population totaled approximately 198 million by the end of 2020. The population distribution is characterized by relative concentrations in basins, plains, and urban areas, in contrast to the sparsely populated mountainous regions. Statistical methods Prior to model construction, to ensure the robustness and interpretability of the analytical results, we constructed an initial set of variables by systematically reviewing existing literature to screen for potential environmental factors associated with the occurrence of HFRS. All candidate variables were entered into the MaxEnt model for a preliminary run, with the number of replicates set to 1. The Jackknife test was subsequently employed to evaluate the contribution and importance of each variable to the model. To prevent model overfitting and potential interference with result interpretation caused by the coexistence of highly correlated variables, we subsequently conducted a multicollinearity test using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis, establishing a threshold of 0.8 (|r| ≥ 0.8)[26]. For pairs of highly correlated variables, selection was prioritized based on contribution metrics derived from the preliminary model run: the variable with the higher contribution was retained, while the lower-contributing variable Page 7/30 was excluded. Ultimately, a final set of variables that were mutually independent and possessed significant explanatory power for HFRS transmission risk was selected to construct the final model. Maximum entropy modeling process Model construction In this study, the Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt, version 3.4.3) model was employed for ecological niche modeling. Based on the principle of maximum entropy, this model predicts the probability of presence in specific habitats by integrating geographic occurrence records of HFRS cases with environmental background points; it is widely recognized as a robust machine learning method characterized by high predictive accuracy[27, 28]. Model training and parameter optimization: To construct a high-precision predictive model, the key eco-environmental factors identified during the screening process were incorporated into the MaxEnt model. In terms of data partitioning, 75% of the HFRS occurrence records were randomly selected as the training set for model calibration, while the remaining 25% were reserved as the test set for model validation[29, 30]. To minimize random errors associated with single simulations and enhance the stability of the results, the model was executed with 10 replicates, and the final output was derived from the average of these 10 runs. Apart from these specific settings, all other parameters were maintained at the software's default values[31]. Model performance evaluation: The predictive performance of the model was evaluated primarily using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)[32]. The AUC values range from 0 to 1, with a value closer to 1 indicating superior predictive performance. Specifically, an AUC of 0.5 represents a random prediction. The performance levels are categorized as follows: 0.5–0.6 is considered poor; 0.7–0.8 is fair; 0.8–0.9 is good; and 0.9–1.0 is excellent[33]. Furthermore, a threshold- dependent binomial test was employed, utilizing the omission rate as a test statistic to comprehensively evaluate the statistical significance of the model and assess the potential for overfitting[34]. Analysis of environmental variable importance To identify the key driving factors influencing the distribution of HFRS, the Jackknife test was employed to quantitatively evaluate the contribution of each environmental variable to the model gain, thereby identifying the dominant variables containing the most critical information[35].Additionally, response curves were utilized to analyze the non-linear response patterns of the predicted probability of HFRS Page 8/30 occurrence to variations in individual variables, thereby elucidating the quantitative relationships between environmental factors and disease risk[34, 36]. Risk zonation and population exposure assessment The output of the MaxEnt model consists of continuous probability values ranging from 0 to 1, representing the environmental suitability for the occurrence of HFRS (i.e., the potential risk). Based on the characteristics of the probability distribution, the risk levels were stratified into three categories: low- risk zones (≤ 0.29), medium-risk zones (0.29–0.45), and high-risk zones (> 0.45). Finally, a spatial overlay analysis was performed using ArcGIS software to integrate the reclassified risk zonation map with population raster data. This process allowed for the quantitative estimation of the size and spatial distribution characteristics of the population exposed to varying risk levels at both the prefectural and regional scales[37]. Furthermore, HFRS cases exhibited pronounced seasonal fluctuations, characterized by a primary peak during the spring-summer period (April–June) and a secondary peak during the autumn-winter period (November–January). In terms of geographic distribution, the Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture in Sichuan Province, along with the Dali Bai Autonomous Prefecture and Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture in Yunnan Province, were identified as the primary high-incidence areas. Collectively, these three regions accounted for 62.60% of the total cases reported in Southwestern China. Demographic analysis indicated that males and farmers aged 20–60 years constituted the primary high-risk groups. The incidence rate among males was 45.01 per 100,000 population, significantly exceeding that among females (1.76 per 100,000 population). Furthermore, significant heterogeneity in incidence rates was observed across prefecture-level cities, with cases predominantly concentrated in mountainous regions and ethnic autonomous prefectures. Read Full License Additional Declarations: No competing interests reported. Page 3/30 Abstract Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) severely burdens China's public health. With its complex topography and rich biodiversity, Southwest China has historically incubated this natural focal disease. Currently, traditional environmental drivers of transmission here are increasingly eclipsed by anthropogenic forces, notably population agglomeration. Driven by these shifting dynamics, HFRS incidence and endemic ranges are expanding, yet systematic, regional-scale assessments remain scarce. Consequently, this study employs ecological niche modeling to map potential high-risk zones. Ultimately, we aim to explore the core mechanisms driving HFRS prevalence amid the complex interplay of natural environments and human activities. Methods Surveillance data of HFRS cases in Southwest China from 2014 to 2023 were obtained from the China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention (CISDCP). A Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model was constructed by integrating occurrence records with multisource environmental variables, including meteorological, socioeconomic, and land cover factors. Model performance was evaluated using the Area Under the Curve (AUC) of the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC), and the Jackknife test was employed to quantify the contribution of each variable. Results The MaxEnt model demonstrated robust predictive performance with a mean AUC of 0.902. Population density was identified as the predominant predictor (73.5% contribution), followed by the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) in May (9.2%) and annual mean temperature (5.8%). Response curves revealed a sigmoidal positive correlation between population density and disease risk. Meteorological factors, such as temperature and precipitation, exhibited non-linear inverted U-shaped or U-shaped relationships, constraining the spatial boundaries of transmission. Human population density acts as the primary amplifier of transmission risk, supporting the human behavior amplification effect in natural focal diseases. papers.title: Hantavirus and Pregnancy: What Obstetricians Need to Know.
papers.abstract: A recent cluster of cases of severe respiratory illness due to Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infection highlights the need for obstetricians to understand hantavirus infection, including its implications during pregnancy. We have summarized English-language reports indexed in PubMed that describe hantavirus infection in pregnancy. Although we did not identify any published cases of ANDV infection in pregnancy, reports of ANDV infection among nonpregnant individuals as well as other types of hantavirus infection in pregnancy can help inform diagnosis, management, and prevention in pregnancy. Patients with hantavirus infection can deteriorate rapidly after the onset of respiratory symptoms and often require supportive care in an intensive care unit. Therefore, it is critical that clinicians have a high index of suspicion for hantavirus infection based largely on travel and exposure history. The primary mode of prevention for hantavirus infection is to avoid contact with rodents and their excreta. Because there are no effective therapies for hantavirus infection, treatment is supportive.

papers.title: Integrated analysis on immunoreactivity and immunogenetics of Hantaan virus glycoprotein epitopes.
papers.abstract: As a bridge between humoral and cellular immunity in the body, CD4+ T cells play an important role in the clearance of Hantaan virus (HTNV) infection. The envelope-anchored glycoprotein (GP) is responsible for orchestrating host cell entry and fusion. In the bioinformatics stage of this study, we assessed 22 dominant B-cell epitopes and 191 T-cell epitopes (including MHC-I and MHC-II restricted) covering MHC genotype frequencies ≥30% in various regions worldwide, using multiple prediction algorithms and HLA population-frequency criteria. Through affinity analysis and molecular docking, the relationship between nonapeptide determinants and 15-mer epitopes suggested that consecutive CD4+ T-cell epitopes may share a nonapeptide that plays a major binding role in multiple HLA genotypes. Sequence alignment of the reported viral variants showed that affinity changes of non-conserved epitopes were tiny in either humoral or cellular immunity. Toxicity and allergenicity screening identified 23 peptides as safe and available to the body. Based on these bioinformatics predictions, we selected candidate peptides for experimental validation. In the wet-lab stage, specialized immunological assays (ELISA and ELISpot) were performed using human peripheral blood samples from vaccinated volunteers, and anti-HTNV humoral and cellular immune epitopes were validated. The results are strongly representative in a certain population and HLA genotypes. Our research is grounded in HTNV GP and provides a theoretical basis for the use of epitopes in the prevention and control of HTNV. More importantly, studies of T-cell and B-cell epitopes from multiple dimensions and perspectives would further deepen the understanding of peptide-based immunotherapy against emerging viral infections and accelerate the development of global public health services.

analysis.background: HTNV infection requires effective immune clearance, with CD4+ T cells bridging humoral and cellular immunity (A1).
analysis.methods: The study used bioinformatic prediction of 22 B‑cell and 191 T‑cell epitopes (A3), affinity analysis and molecular docking to identify shared nonapeptide determinants (A4), toxicity/allergenicity screening of 23 peptides (A6), selection of candidates for testing (A7), and ELISA/ELISpot assays on human peripheral blood from vaccinated volunteers (A8).

analysis.contribution: The work provides a theoretical basis for using HTNV GP epitopes in prevention and control (A10) and highlights how multidimensional epitope studies can advance peptide‑based immunotherapy and global public‑health preparedness (A11).
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, limiting detail on experimental design, sample size, and quantitative outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HTNV infection relies on CD4+ T‑cell mediated clearance (A1). Methods: Bioinformatic prediction of B‑ and T‑cell epitopes, affinity docking, safety screening, and ELISA/ELISpot validation on vaccinated human samples were performed (A3‑A8). Results: Non‑conserved epitopes showed minimal affinity changes, 23 peptides were safe, and predicted epitopes were experimentally validated, representing certain HLA genotypes (A5‑A9). Contribution: The study offers a theoretical basis for HTNV GP‑based vaccines and underscores the value of multidimensional epitope research for immunotherapy and public‑health (A10‑A11). Limitations: Only abstract data are provided, restricting insight into detailed methods and results.

papers.title: Immunopathogenic insights into members of the class Bunyaviricetes: a comparative review of emerging zoonotic threats.
papers.abstract: The class Bunyaviricetes encompasses a diverse group of vector- and rodent-borne viruses, many of which are major human pathogens causing severe and often lethal diseases worldwide. These include Lassa fever virus (Arenaviridae), hantaviruses such as Hantaan and Andes viruses (Hantaviridae), Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (Nairoviridae), La Crosse and Oropouche viruses (Peribunyaviridae), and Rift Valley fever, severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, and Toscana viruses (Phenuiviridae). Clinical syndromes range from hemorrhagic fever with multiorgan failure, vascular leak, and shock to acute encephalitis and severe respiratory distress. Despite their public health impact, safe and effective vaccines or targeted therapeutics are lacking for most bunyaviricetes diseases, leaving supportive care as the primary intervention. This review provides a comparative analysis of the immunopathogenesis of major human-pathogenic bunyaviricetes, highlighting shared and virus-specific strategies for innate immune evasion, cytokine modulation, and host cell targeting. Severe disease often arises from viral interference with key sensing pathways, such as RIG-I/MDA5 and downstream IRF and NF-κB signaling, which either suppresses interferon responses or leads to dysregulated inflammation. By integrating molecular, immunological, and clinical insights, we outline how these immune-virus interactions shape disease trajectory and severity. Understanding these mechanisms is critical for guiding the rational design of vaccines, antivirals, and immunomodulatory therapies, and for strengthening preparedness against these persistent zoonotic threats.

analysis.background: The class Bunyaviricetes includes diverse vector- and rodent‑borne viruses that cause severe, often lethal human disease worldwide.
analysis.main_directions: The review compares immunopathogenic mechanisms across major human‑pathogenic bunyaviricetes, focusing on innate immune evasion, cytokine modulation, and host‑cell targeting.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The class Bunyaviricetes includes diverse vector- and rodent-borne viruses causing severe, often lethal disease worldwide. Main directions: The review compares immunopathogenic mechanisms across major human-pathogenic bunyaviricetes, emphasizing innate immune evasion, cytokine modulation, and host-cell targeting. Current state: These viruses disrupt RIG-I/MDA5 sensing and IRF/NF-κB signaling, suppressing interferon or causing dysregulated inflammation. Gaps: Safe, effective vaccines and targeted therapeutics are lacking, leaving supportive care as the primary intervention. Future research: Translate mechanistic insights into rational vaccine, antiviral, and immunomodulatory development and strengthen surveillance and preparedness.

analysis_zh.background: Bunyaviricetes纲包括多样的媒介和啮齿动物传播病毒,导致全球范围内严重且常致命的人类疾病。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述比较主要人类致病性Bunyaviricetes的免疫致病机制,重点关注先天免疫逃逸、细胞因子调节以及宿主细胞靶向。
analysis_zh.current_state: 当前证据显示,这些病毒破坏RIG‐I/MDA5感知及其下游IRF/NF‐κB信号通路,抑制干扰素应答或引发失调的炎症。
analysis_zh.gaps: 对大多数Bunyaviricetes感染仍缺乏安全、有效的疫苗和靶向治疗手段,支持治疗成为唯一选择。
analysis_zh.future_research: 进一步工作应将机制性认识转化为合理的疫苗设计、抗病毒药物开发和免疫调节策略,并加强对这些人畜共患威胁的监测与防备。

papers.title: Hantavirus infections in Southeastern Europe - Epidemiology, outbreak dynamics, and One Health preparedness: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Human-pathogenic orthohantaviruses are significant rodent-borne zoonotic pathogens in Europe. Southeastern Europe (SEE) is a distinct endemic region where Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) and Puumala virus (PUUV) co-circulate, causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) of varying severity. This narrative review synthesizes the epidemiology, transmission dynamics, clinical characteristics, ecological drivers, and public health challenges of hantavirus infections across SEE, identifying priorities for regional preparedness. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from their inception through June 2026, supplementing with reference screening. Regional epidemiological patterns were assessed descriptively using national surveillance data, European surveillance reports, published studies, and available population-based incidence estimates. Long-term surveillance reveals persistent endemic transmission with significant geographic and interannual heterogeneity. Slovenia and Croatia exhibit the highest cumulative burden and most pronounced periods of increased HFRS activity. Several years-2008, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023-showed partially synchronized increases across multiple neighboring countries. These patterns align with shared ecological influences, including rodent population fluctuations, mast-seeding events, and climatic variability. However, local ecology, human exposure, and differences in surveillance capacity modify their magnitude. The coexistence of generally milder PUUV-associated disease and more severe DOBV-associated HFRS further distinguishes SEE's clinical landscape. Therefore, hantavirus epidemiology in SEE is best understood as an interconnected regional ecological system. Integrated human, animal, environmental, and genomic surveillance within a coordinated One Health framework is crucial for improving outbreak prediction, cross-border preparedness, and future disease control.

Southeastern Europe (SEE) is a distinct endemic region where Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) and Puumala virus (PUUV) co-circulate, causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) of varying severity. This narrative review synthesizes the epidemiology, transmission dynamics, clinical characteristics, ecological drivers, and public health challenges of hantavirus infections across SEE, identifying priorities for regional preparedness. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from their inception through June 2026, supplementing with reference screening. Regional epidemiological patterns were assessed descriptively using national surveillance data, European surveillance reports, published studies, and available population-based incidence estimates. Long-term surveillance reveals persistent endemic transmission with significant geographic and interannual heterogeneity. Slovenia and Croatia exhibit the highest cumulative burden and most pronounced periods of increased HFRS activity. Several years-2008, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2019, 2021, and 2023-showed partially synchronized increases across multiple neighboring countries. These patterns align with shared ecological influences, including rodent population fluctuations, mast-seeding events, and climatic variability. However, local ecology, human exposure, and differences in surveillance capacity modify their magnitude. The coexistence of generally milder PUUV-associated disease and more severe DOBV-associated HFRS further distinguishes SEE's clinical landscape. Therefore, hantavirus epidemiology in SEE is best understood as an interconnected regional ecological system. Integrated human, animal, environmental, and genomic surveillance within a coordinated One Health framework is crucial for improving outbreak prediction, cross-border preparedness, and future disease control.

Keywords: Orthohantavirus, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, Dobrava– Belgrade virus, Puumala virus, Southeastern Europe, zoonoses, One Health approach. 4 INTRODUCTION Human-pathogenic orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae) are among the most important rodent-borne zoonotic viruses worldwide and are responsible for the clinical syndromes collectively referred to as hantavirus disease [1,2]. Throughout this review, the term orthohantavirus is used when referring to the virus taxonomy, whereas hantavirus disease and related clinical terminology are retained for consistency with established medical nomenclature. In Eurasia, hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), whereas in the Americas they cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS, also known as HPS) [3,4]. Their public health significance extends beyond their clinical impact and reflects their remarkable ability to persist silently within particular small-mammal reservoir hosts, amplify under favorable ecological conditions, and periodically emerge as geographically focal outbreaks in human populations [5–7]. Consequently, hantavirus disease represents a paradigmatic example of a zoonotic pathogen shaped by complex interactions among viral biology, reservoir ecology, land use, and climatic conditions [6–8]. In Europe, the epidemiological and public-health landscape is dominated by Old World orthohantaviruses, particularly Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava–Belgrade virus (DOBV), that vary in reservoir associations, ecological niches, geographical distribution, and typical disease severity, yet together account for the majority of the regional HFRS burden [4,9,10]. Southeastern Europe (SEE) occupies a unique position within the European orthohantavirus landscape and cannot be viewed merely as a southern extension of the PUUV-dominated ecosystems of Central and Northern Europe. Rather it represents one of the few European macro-regions where highly pathogenic DOBV lineages and less virulent PUUV strains coexist in shared ecological and clinical space, thereby contributing to a heterogeneous regional risk signature that cannot be understood with respect to northern-European nephropathia epidemica models alone [4,9]. As no single definition of SEE exists, for the purposes of this review the region comprises Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, and Slovenia. SEE countries have played an important role in hantavirus research, as DOBV was first identified in the former Yugoslavia [10]. The region remains characterized by endemic circulation of orthohantaviruses in both human populations and rodent reservoirs, with marked 5 geographic heterogeneity and localized transmission foci. Thus, human infections and evidence of viral circulation have been documented across all countries included in the study [11–16] . Although clinical reporting remains limited in some parts of the region, there is evidence of ongoing viral circulation throughout. Renewed interest in hantavirus disease across SEE has been driven by climatic variability, changing reservoir ecology, land-use change, and evolving human exposure patterns, all of which contribute to dynamic transmission risk across the region [5,17–19]. Therefore, hantavirus disease in SEE should be interpreted not as a static endemicity problem, but as a dynamic interface between reservoir ecology, environmental change, and human activities. Accordingly, this review synthesizes current evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical characteristics, ecological drivers, and public health challenges across SEE, with particular emphasis on regional outbreak patterns and cross-border epidemiological dynamics. Search strategy and data sources This review was based on a structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify literature relevant to orthohantavirus disease in Southeastern Europe. Searches covered publications available from database inception until June 2026 and combined terms including “hantavirus”, “orthohantavirus”, “hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome”, “Southeastern Europe”, “Balkans”, and the names of individual countries within the study region. Additional relevant publications were identified through manual screening of reference lists of eligible articles. The review focuses on the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, transmission dynamics, and public health implications of human hantavirus infections in Southeastern Europe. As this is a narrative review, studies were selected according to their relevance to the scope of the manuscript rather than through formal systematic-review methodology. The epidemiological data presented in Table 2 were compiled from multiple complementary sources, including annual surveillance reports of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), official national public health reports, and country-specific datasets provided or verified by collaborating public health experts where available. Given the heterogeneity of surveillance systems, reporting practices, and laboratory confirmation procedures across countries, epidemiological 6 data were interpreted descriptively. The primary data source for each country is summarized in Table S1. For countries with ECDC-derived data, EU-level surveillance through TESSy is available from 2008 onward; therefore, our comparative analysis covers 2008–2024, while earlier years are reported as N/A. Heyman et al. independently documented laboratory-diagnosed hantavirus infections in Greece, Slovenia, Romania, and Bulgaria during 2005–2007 [20]. We cite these findings as evidence of earlier hantavirus activity, but do not combine them with the ECDC or national data because the two sources are based on different surveillance approaches. Annual incidence rates were calculated as: Incidence (per 100,000 population) = (annual number of reported HFRS cases / corresponding annual mid-year population estimate) × 100,000. Annual country-specific mid-year population estimates were obtained from the World Bank DataBank, World Development Indicators (indicator SP.POP.TOTL) and matched to the corresponding surveillance year for each country. World Bank data were accessed on July 9 2026 [21]. Epidemiology of hantavirus infections in Southeastern Europe HFRS has been recognized in SEE for more than half a century, and the region remains a well-established endemic region characterized by sporadic cases each year punctuated by periodic epidemics [9]. A distinct north-south gradient is evident across the region, with PUUV being relatively more common in the northern part of the region, and DOBV predominating in the southern Balkans [9,22]. SEE is also the cradle of DOBV taxonomy: the prototype Dobrava strain was recovered from yellow- necked mouse (A. flavicollis) in Slovenia, while Belgrade virus was isolated from a fatal HFRS case in Serbia, with both subsequently confirmed as genetically identical [10,23]. DOBV and PUUV co-circulate widely across the Balkans, with generally moderate reported regional incidence but subject to marked interannual variability driven by multi-annual rodent population cycles [19]. Outbreaks typically follow mast-seeding events and favorable climatic conditions, including winters that enhance rodent survival and reproduction [4,6,7]. 7 Subclinical infections are common, with estimated subclinical-to-clinical ratios ranging from 5:1 to 20:1, resulting in substantial under-ascertainment, particularly of mild PUUV-associated disease [19,24,25]. Seroepidemiological surveys indicate substantial background exposure with a clear geographic gradient: overall seroprevalence has been estimated at approximately 6% in BiH, approximately 4% in Greece (range 0 to 14% by county), 3.1% in Bulgaria, 1.7% in Slovenia, and 1.6% in Croatia, with higher rates reported among occupationally exposed populations and local foci [9,14,25–29]. Evidence of viral circulation has been documented across the SEE region, although the dominant virus and disease burden vary according to local ecology, rodent-host distribution, and surveillance intensity (Table 1). Albania and Kosovo were not included in the comparative surveillance analysis presented in Table 2 because continuous annual surveillance data were not publicly available for inclusion; therefore, the information presented for these countries is based primarily on the available published evidence. BiH has been a major endemic focus of hantavirus infections in Europe for more than 50 years. Outbreaks have been documented since 1967, with large epidemics in the former Yugoslavia during 1986-1987 and 1989, involving more than 1,000 reported cases, and further outbreaks in 1995 and 2002, the latter implicating PUUV, DOBV and untyped serotypes [30–34] . Following the 2002 epidemic, hantavirus infections continued to occur regularly in BiH, with at least one confirmed case reported annually between 2005 and 2024 (Table 2). Although annual case numbers were generally low, pronounced peaks were observed in 2014, 2017, and 2021, supporting the persistence of endemic circulation with periodic outbreaks. While the majority of reported cases originate from central and northeastern Bosnia, the distribution of rodent reservoirs and serological evidence of exposure indicate that hantavirus circulation extends beyond these recognized endemic foci [27,35]. Consequently, the geographic distribution of infection may be broader than that indicated by routine surveillance data. In Croatia, both DOBV and PUUV contribute to disease burden, with a notable military outbreak in 1995, and large epidemics in 2002, 2012, 2014, 2017, and 2021. Notably, the 2012 Medvednica outbreak was linked to exceptionally high PUUV infection rates in bank voles, while the 2017 (≈389 notified cases) and 2021 (≈334 8 cases) outbreaks were the largest on record and extended into Adriatic-coastal and other areas previously considered non-endemic [18,36,37]. Serbia has reported HFRS since 1961, with Belgrade virus characterized during a 1989 epidemic and subsequent molecular confirmation of DOBV circulation foci in western and central regions [10,38,39] . Serbian national surveillance demonstrates persistent endemic HFRS activity, with generally low annual incidence punctuated by occasional increases in reported cases. In Greece, serological evidence dates to 1981, with 0–4 HFRS cases reported annually in recent years and an estimated case-fatality of approximately 9% among hospitalized patients, a figure derived from severely ill cases and therefore an overestimate of the overall rate [14,40]. DOBV (genotype Dobrava, hosted by A. flavicollis) predominates, with 80% of all cases occurring in endemic foci in the Rhodope and Pindos mountains near the northern borders and no cases reported from southern Greece or the islands, whereas PUUV is also endemic but accounts for far fewer recognized cases [10,14] . Despite relatively low annual notification rates, the persistence of endemic foci and serological evidence of exposure indicate continuous viral circulation, emphasizing the importance of maintaining surveillance in northern Greece. Bulgaria has recorded HFRS since the 1950s, mainly across the Rila-Pirin-Rodopi massifs of the southwest, where phylogenetically related DOBV strains circulate in Apodemus mice, confirming local rodent reservoirs [9,10,16]. Although reported incidence has remained consistently low, the continued detection of DOBV in both rodents and human cases supports persistent endemic transmission rather than sporadic viral introduction. Albania likewise has confirmed hantavirus circulation through genetic detection in rodent hosts [12,41–43], while Kosovo reports severe DOBV-associated HFRS, with documented population seroconversion in endemic zones and severe sporadic cases [15,44,45]. Slovenia represents one of the most affected countries in SEE, experiencing recurrent large-scale outbreaks and the highest incidence rates recorded in the region, particularly during 2012, 2019, and 2021. In contrast, Montenegro reports relatively few cases but periodically reaches among the highest annual incidence rates in SEE 9 owing to its small population size, illustrating the importance of interpreting incidence alongside absolute case numbers [46] . North Macedonia has reported only sporadic cases in recent years, although limited surveillance coverage makes it difficult to determine the true extent of endemic circulation [11]. Hantavirus infections in Romania remain rare but endemic, with sporadic cases reported over the past two decades, primarily caused by DOBV [4,13] . Despite the low number of reported cases, increasing recognition through improved diagnostics and surveillance suggests that hantavirus infections may be more widespread than previously appreciated. The comparative analysis of 20-year surveillance data presented in Table 2, based on long-term national surveillance data and complemented by ECDC surveillance reports and published national epidemiological studies, further illustrates the heterogeneous yet interconnected epidemiological landscape of hantavirus infections in SEE. Current state: Long-term surveillance shows persistent endemic transmission with significant geographic and interannual heterogeneity; Slovenia and Croatia bear the highest cumulative burden, and the coexistence of milder PUUV-associated disease and more severe DOBV-associated HFRS defines SEE’s clinical landscape. Gaps: Surveillance capacity differences, local ecological and exposure variations, and limited integration of human, animal, environmental, and genomic data constrain accurate outbreak prediction and cross-border preparedness. Future research: Implement integrated One Health surveillance combining human, animal, environmental, and genomic data to improve outbreak prediction, cross-border preparedness, and disease control in SEE.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 在东南欧的感染 - 流行病学、暴发动态与 One Health 准备:叙述性综述。

analysis_zh.background: 人源致病的 正汉坦病毒 是欧洲重要的啮齿动物传播的动物源性病原体,东南欧 (SEE) 独特地共存循环的多布拉瓦-贝尔格莱德病毒 (DOBV) 和 普马拉病毒 (PUUV),导致 肾综合征出血热(HFRS),其严重程度各异。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述综合了 汉坦病毒 感染在 SEE 的流行病学、传播动力学、临床特征、生态驱动因素和公共卫生挑战,突出持续的地方性传播、地理和年际异质性,以及与啮齿动物种群波动、阔叶树丰产和气候变异部分同步的暴发高峰。
analysis_zh.current_state: 长期监测显示,地方性传播持续存在,且存在显著的地理和年际异质性;斯洛文尼亚和克罗地亚承担最高的累计负担,且较轻的 PUUV 相关疾病与更严重的 DOBV 相关 HFRS 共存,构成 SEE 的临床格局。
analysis_zh.gaps: 监测能力差异、当地生态和暴露差异,以及人、动物、环境和基因组数据整合有限,限制了对暴发的准确预测和跨境应急准备。
analysis_zh.future_research: 在 SEE 实施融合人、动物、环境和基因组数据的 One Health 综合监测,以提升暴发预测、跨境应急准备和疾病控制。

full_text_sections.full_text: RAZAFINDRALAMBO Nadia Kaloina ARENAVIRUS ET HANTAVIRUS CHEZ LES PETITS MAMMIFERES SAUVAGES TERRESTRES DE MADAGASCAR IDENTIFIES PAR RT-PCR Thèse de Doctorat en Médecine Vétérinaire UNIVERSITE D’ANTANANARIVO FACULTE DE MEDECINE DEPARTEMENT D’ENSEINGNEMENT DES SCIENCES ET DE MEDECINE VETERINAIRES ANNEE : 2011 N° :064 ARENAVIRUS ET HANTAVIRUS CHEZ LES PETITS MAMMIFERES SAUVAGES TERRESTRES DE MADAGASCAR IDENTIFIES PAR RT-PCR THESE Présentée et soutenue publiquement le 16 septembre 2011 à Antananarivo par Mademoiselle RAZAFINDRALAMBO Nadia Kaloina Née le 30 Septembre 1988 à Soavinandriana Antananarivo Pour obtenir le grade de << DOCTEUR EN MEDECINE VETERINAIRE >> (Diplôme d’Etat) Directeur de thèse : Professeur RASAMINDRAKOTROKA Andry MEMBRES DU JURY Président : Professeur RASAMINDRAKOTROKA Andry Juges : Professeur RANDRIANJAFISAMINDRAKOTROKA Nantenaina Soa Professeur RAKOTOZANDRINDRAINY Raphaël Rapporteur : Dr RASOLOFO RAZANAMPARANY Voahangy DEDICACE Je dédie cette thèse : A DIEU Tout Puissant : qui m’a donné la vie et m’a accordé la chance de faire cette thèse. Qu’Il nous accorde sa grâce. « Je t’instruirai et te montrerai la voie que tu dois suivre ; Je te conseillerai, J’aurai le regard sur toi » Psaumes 328 A mes parents : pour tant d’année de sacrifice vos encouragements, votre soutien moral et matériel et votre optimisme dans la vie, m’ont marqué, des qualités qui ont fait de vous des parents exemplaires. Je n’ai pas le mot pour dire ce que je ressens. Veuillez trouvez dans cet humble ouvrage les récompenses de vos efforts. Ce travail est le modeste témoignage de toute mon affection et mon profond respect. Qu’il soit le témoin de mon immense reconnaissance. Que Dieu le Tout Puissant vous garde. Amen A mes sœurs : pour leur support et encouragement, recevez ma tendre affection. Que l’esprit de fraternité nous anime pour toujours. A mes oncles et mes tantes paternels et maternels, à toutes les familles : Je n’ai rien à vous offrir en guise de récompenses. Que la bénédiction de Dieu vous accompagne durant toute votre vie pour qu’Il vous donne mille fois plus que ce que vous avez donné. A mes amis A tous ceux qui ont contribué de loin ou de près à la réalisation de ce travail. A NOTRE MAITRE DIRECTEUR ET PRESIDENT DE THESE Monsieur le Docteur RASAMINDRAKOTROKA Andry Professeur Titulaire d’Enseignement Supérieur et de la Recherche en Immunologie à la Faculté de Médecine d’Antananarivo. « Vous avez accepté de diriger cette thèse et vous avez accueilli sans reserve et avec bienveillance malgré vos incompréhensibles obligations. Vous nous faites aussi l’honneur d’accepter de présider notre thèse. Veuillez trouver à travers ce travail l’expression de notre profonde gratitude » A NOS MAITRES ET HONORABLES JUGES DE THESE Monsieur le Docteur RANDRIANJAFISAMINDRAKOTROKA Nantenaina Soa Professeur Titulaire d’Enseignement Supérieur et de la Recherche en Anatomie Pathologique à la Faculté de Médecine d’Antananarivo. Monsieur le Docteur RAKOTOZANDRINDRAINY Raphaël Professeur Spécialiste en Microbiologie et Parasitologie à l’Ecole Supérieure des Sciences Agronomiques. Enseignant à la Faculté de Médecine d’Antananarivo et au Département d’Enseignement des Sciences et de Médecine Vétérinaires. Nous vous remercions d’avoir accepté de juger ce travail, un peu éloigné de vos préoccupations habituelles. Veuillez bien trouver ici le témoignage de notre respectueuse reconnaissance. A NOTRE RAPPORTEUR DE THESE : Madame le Docteur RASOLOFO RAZANAMPARANY Voahangy Chef de l’Unité de Mycobactéries à l’Institut Pasteur de Madagascar Vous avez bien voulu nous aider dans l’élaboration de ce travail malgré vos lourdes préoccupations. Ce travail que vous nous avez confié est aussi le fruit de votre immense expérience. Nous vous exprimons notre profonde reconnaissance. A NOTRE MAITRE ET DOYEN DE LA FACULTE DE MEDECINE D’ANTANANARIVO Monsieur le Professeur RAPELANORO RABENJA Fahafahantsoa Veuillez recevoir l’expression de notre haute considération. A MES ENCADREURS Monsieur le Docteur Jean-Marc REYNES Monsieur le Docteur Jean-Michel HERAUD Sincères remerciements. A TOUS NOS MAITRES ET PROFESSEURS DE LA FACULTE DE MEDECINE D’ANTANANARIVO - DEPARTEMENT D’ENSEIGNEMENT DES SCIENCES ET DE MEDECINE VETERINAIRES. Notre reconnaissance pour tous les enseignements que vous nous avez prodigués. A TOUT LE PERSONNEL ADMINISTRATIF ET TECHNIQUE DE LA FACULTE DE MEDECINE D’ANTANANARIVO. Merci infiniment. analysis.background: The thesis investigates the presence of arenavirus and hantavirus in wild small terrestrial mammals of Madagascar, a topic relevant for understanding zoonotic virus reservoirs.
analysis.methods: The study screened small terrestrial mammals from Madagascar for arenavirus and hantavirus using RT‑PCR, but sampling design, number of specimens, and laboratory protocols are not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: No quantitative findings or detection rates are reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.contribution: The work contributes baseline surveillance data by documenting the application of molecular detection for arenavirus and hantavirus in Malagasy wildlife, informing future ecological and public‑health studies.
analysis.limitations: The supplied evidence contains only title and front‑matter material; detailed methods, results, and discussion are not reported, preventing assessment of sample size, geographic coverage, or statistical analysis.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The thesis examines arenavirus and hantavirus in wild small terrestrial mammals of Madagascar, important for zoonotic risk. Methods: Mammals were screened by RT‑PCR, but sampling details are not reported. Results: No detection data are provided. Contribution: Provides baseline molecular surveillance of these viruses in Malagasy wildlife. Limitations: Only title and front‑matter are available; methods, results, and conclusions are not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title: Integrated Analysis of Human Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome Cases and Rodent Hantavirus Surveillance in Zhejiang Province, China, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) and Hantaan orthohantavirus (HTNV), remains a neglected rodent-borne zoonosis with persistent residual spillover risk in low-incidence regions of China. This study assessed human HFRS occurrence and small-mammal hantavirus surveillance signals in small-mammal hosts across Zhejiang Province, China, in 2025. Reported human cases were obtained from the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System, and animal host surveillance was conducted at five designated monitoring sites. A total of 107 HFRS cases were reported, occurring year-round with peaks in June and December and showing spatial heterogeneity, presenting a predominance of males, adults aged ≥40 years, and farmers. Animal host surveillance captured 617 small mammals (566 rodents and 51 shrews) from 15,457 valid trap-nights, with Apodemus agrarius (30.31%) and Rattus norvegicus (29.98%) as the dominant species. Sixteen animals were positive for hantavirus RNA and/or antibody, including 12 for hantavirus RNA and 6 antibody-positive animals; two were positive for both markers. Positive animals were detected in multiple species, including Niviventer confucianus, R. norvegicus, Rattus losea, A. agrarius, Suncus murinus, and Rattus tanezumi. Human incidence, small-mammal density, host species composition, and hantavirus-positive rates were not fully concordant across surveillance sites. Our findings reveal sustained cryptic orthohantavirus circulation in low-endemic Zhejiang, highlighting that integrated human-reservoir One Health surveillance is indispensable for precise spillover risk prediction and targeted zoonotic disease intervention.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV) and Hantaan orthohantavirus (HTNV), is a neglected rodent‑borne zoonosis with persistent spillover risk in low‑incidence regions of China.
analysis.methods: The study assessed human HFRS occurrence and small‑mammal hantavirus surveillance across Zhejiang Province in 2025, using case data from the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System and trapping at five monitoring sites, capturing 617 small mammals over 15,457 trap‑nights.
analysis.results: A total of 107 HFRS cases were reported year‑round with peaks in June and December, predominately among male farmers aged ≥40 years; 617 mammals (566 rodents, 51 shrews) were trapped, with Apodemus agrarius (30.31 %) and Rattus norvegicus (29.98 %) dominant; 16 animals were hantavirus‑positive (12 RNA, 6 antibody, 2 both) across multiple species; human incidence and rodent density/composition were not fully concordant across sites.
analysis.contribution: The findings reveal sustained cryptic orthohantavirus circulation in low‑endemic Zhejiang and highlight that integrated One Health surveillance is essential for precise spillover risk prediction and targeted zoonotic disease intervention.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available, so detailed methods, statistical analyses, and broader context are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by SEOV and HTNV is a neglected rodent‑borne zoonosis with ongoing spillover risk in low‑incidence China. Methods: Human case data from the national surveillance system and trapping at five sites in Zhejiang (2025) yielded 617 mammals from 15,457 trap‑nights. Results: 107 HFRS cases occurred year‑round (peaks June, December) mainly in male farmers ≥40 y; rodents were dominated by A. agrarius (30.31 %) and R. norvegicus (29.98 %); 16 animals were hantavirus‑positive (12 RNA, 6 antibody, 2 both) across several species; human and rodent metrics were not fully aligned across sites. Contribution: The study shows cryptic orthohantavirus circulation and stresses integrated One Health surveillance for risk prediction and intervention. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided, limiting detail on methods and analyses.

papers.title_zh: 中国浙江省2025年人类肾综合征出血热病例与啮齿动物汉坦病毒监测的综合分析

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS),由首尔病毒(SEOV)和汉滩病毒(HTNV)引起,是一种被忽视的啮齿动物源人畜共患病,在中国低发地区仍存在持续的跨种传播风险。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究评估了2025年浙江省的人类肾综合征出血热(HFRS)发生情况及小型哺乳动物汉坦病毒监测,使用国家法定传染病监测系统的病例数据,并在五个监测点进行捕捉,共捕获617只小型哺乳动物,累计捕鼠夜15,457夜。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果显示,低流行地区浙江存在持续的隐匿性正汉坦病毒传播,并强调综合One Health监测对于精准预测跨种传播风险和开展有针对性的动物源性疾病干预至关重要。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,因而未报告详细方法、统计分析及更广泛的背景信息。

papers.title: Cardiopulmonary Failure in Hantavirus Disease: Mechanisms, Recognition, and ECMO-Based Management.
papers.abstract: Background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), also designated hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, is caused by New World hantaviruses, principally Sin Nombre virus in North America and Andes virus in South America. The syndrome is characterized by rapidly progressive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and myocardial depression, with case fatality rates of 25% to 40%. A 2026 outbreak aboard an expedition cruise ship in the South Atlantic, comprising 13 cases and three deaths, confirmed that Andes virus can be transmitted between humans in a confined setting remote from the rodent reservoir. Methods: Virological, pathophysiological, clinical, and therapeutic aspects of HPS were reviewed, with particular emphasis on cardiopulmonary mechanisms. Sources were identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with priority given to original research articles, clinical series, and controlled trials published through 2025. Literature published in English and Spanish was included. Results: Pathogenic hantaviruses enter endothelial cells and platelets via αvβ3 integrins, disrupting the VEGF-VEGFR2 signaling axis and rendering endothelial cells hypersensitive to physiological VEGF concentrations. Expansion of CD8+ T cells and activated macrophages releases TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, and nitric oxide, amplifying microvascular permeability and contributing to myocardial depression. Autopsy studies demonstrate direct hantaviral myocarditis with viral antigen in cardiac endothelium and interstitial macrophages. Transpulmonary thermodilution confirms simultaneous hypovolemia, reduced global ejection fraction, and elevated extravascular lung water. Because the incubation period is long and the cardiopulmonary phase is substantially immune-mediated, seroconversion precedes rather than follows clinical deterioration, which preserves the diagnostic utility of IgM serology in a disease that can kill within 48 h. VA-ECMO initiated at the first signs of cardiopulmonary decompensation has reported survival rates approaching 80% in selected experienced centers. No antiviral has demonstrated efficacy in controlled trials during the cardiopulmonary phase, and no licensed vaccine exists. Conclusions: HPS produces a mixed shock state through increased microvascular permeability, T cell-mediated immunopathology, and direct myocarditis. Management follows a stepwise algorithm: suspected HPS triggers immediate complete blood count with peripheral blood smear and concurrent hantavirus IgM serology and RT-PCR, followed by ICU admission, conservative fluid resuscitation guided by transpulmonary thermodilution, and early contact with an ECMO-capable center at the first sign of rising lactate, falling cardiac index, refractory shock, arrhythmia, or rapid oxygenation failure.

analysis.background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is a severe disease caused by New World hantaviruses such as Sin Nombre and Andes virus, marked by rapidly progressive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and myocardial depression (A1, A2).
analysis.main_directions: The review examines endothelial and immune mechanisms (αvβ3 integrin entry, VEGF signaling disruption, cytokine release), direct myocarditis, diagnostic strategies (IgM serology, RT‑PCR, transpulmonary thermodilution), and ECMO-based management (A7–A12).
analysis.current_state: Evidence shows hantavirus infection induces endothelial hyperpermeability, T‑cell–mediated inflammation, and myocardial depression, with ECMO survival rates up to 80% in experienced centers, yet no antiviral or vaccine has proven efficacy (A7–A13).
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include the lack of effective antivirals or licensed vaccines, limited controlled trial data, and uncertainty about optimal ECMO timing and protocols, especially after the 2026 cruise‑ship outbreak demonstrating human‑to‑human transmission (A3, A13).
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritize antiviral and vaccine development, multicenter ECMO outcome studies, refined diagnostic algorithms incorporating early serology and hemodynamic monitoring, and surveillance of nosocomial transmission (A3, A12, A13).

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 疾病的心肺衰竭:机制、识别与基于 ECMO 的管理。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征(HPS)是一种由新世界汉坦病毒病毒(如Sin Nombre和安第斯病毒)引起的重症疾病,特征为快速进展的非心源性肺水肿和心肌抑制(A1,A2)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述审查内皮和免疫机制(αvβ3 整合素进入、VEGF 信号破坏、细胞因子释放)、直接心肌炎、诊断策略(IgM血清学、RT‐PCR、经肺热稀释),以及基于 ECMO 的管理(A7–A12)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 证据表明 汉坦病毒 感染导致内皮通透性增高、T 细胞介导的炎症以及心肌抑制,在经验丰富的中心 ECMO 存活率可达 80%,但尚无抗病毒药物或疫苗显示有效性(A7–A13)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 关键缺口包括缺乏有效的抗病毒药物或获批疫苗、受限的对照试验数据,以及对最佳 ECMO 时机和方案的不确定性,尤其是在 2026 年邮轮爆发显示人际传播之后(A3,A13)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应优先开展抗病毒药物和疫苗研发、多中心 ECMO 结局研究、结合早期血清学和血流动力学监测的精细诊断算法,以及对院内传播的监测(A3,A12,A13)。

papers.title: Hantavirus: A focused review for the emergency medicine clinician.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Andes virus (ANDV), a form of hantavirus, is a potentially fatal disease with several cases recently reported aboard an expedition cruise ship in April and May 2026. OBJECTIVE: This focused narrative review provides a focused overview of the epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of hantavirus infection, including ANDV, for the emergency clinician. DISCUSSION: Human infections with hantavirus primarily occur through contact with aerosolized particles of saliva, feces, or urine of infected rodents or through touching contaminated surfaces. A recent outbreak of ANDV has demonstrated human-to-human transmission in the setting of close, prolonged contact. The incubation period ranges between 4 and 42 days. As hantaviruses target the endothelium of capillaries and small vessels, patients may develop hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, predominantly associated with hantaviruses found in Europe and Asia or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, mainly associated with hantaviruses in the Americas. Both hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus with pulmonary syndrome present initially with a non-specific viral prodrome (e.g., fever, chills, malaise, myalgias). Following this prodrome, patients with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome can demonstrate coagulation abnormalities and change in urine output with renal dysfunction, while hantavirus with pulmonary syndrome presents with cardiopulmonary symptoms with cough, dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypotension that may progress to respiratory failure and cardiogenic shock. Diagnosis incorporates ELISA assay to detect IgG and IgM antibodies. Patients with concern for ANDV should be isolated in a private room (preferably a negative pressure room). Airborne and contact precautions are recommended; strategies similar to those employed for managing patients with viral hemorrhagic fever may be considered. Treatment is primarily supportive, including resuscitation with intravenous fluids and vasopressors, respiratory support (e.g., supplemental oxygen, noninvasive ventilation, endotracheal intubation), antipyretics and analgesics, and hemorrhage control as needed. Mechanical ventilation, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and hemodialysis may be necessary. CONCLUSION: Hantavirus may initially present with a non-specific viral prodrome, but travel and social history should prompt greater diagnostic suspicion. Patients are managed similarly to those with other viral hemorrhagic fevers.

analysis.background: Recent cases of Andes virus (ANDV) aboard a cruise ship in 2026 have raised concern for emergency clinicians.
analysis.main_directions: The review outlines epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of hantavirus infections, emphasizing endothelial targeting and distinct syndromes (HFRS vs HPS).
analysis.current_state: Human infection occurs mainly via aerosolized rodent excreta, with established diagnostic ELISA testing and primarily supportive care.
analysis.gaps: The recent demonstration of human‑to‑human transmission of ANDV highlights limited data on transmission dynamics and lack of specific antivirals.
analysis.future_research: Further surveillance of transmission patterns, evaluation of antiviral or vaccine candidates, and clarification of incubation variability are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Recent cruise‑ship cases of Andes virus prompted this review. Main directions: It covers epidemiology, clinical syndromes, diagnosis, and supportive management of hantavirus. Current state: Transmission is rodent‑borne, ELISA is used for diagnosis, and care is supportive. Gaps: Human‑to‑human spread of ANDV is newly documented, and specific therapies are lacking. Future research: Surveillance of transmission, trials of antivirals or vaccines, and better definition of incubation periods are required.

analysis_zh.background: 2026年在一艘邮轮上出现的安第斯病毒(ANDV)近期病例引起了急诊临床医生的关注。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了汉坦病毒感染的流行病学、临床表现、诊断和管理,强调靶向内皮以及不同综合征(肾综合征出血热 vs 汉坦病毒肺综合征)。

analysis_zh.gaps: 近期安第斯病毒的人际传播证据凸显了传播动力学数据有限以及缺乏特异性抗病毒药物的现状。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要进一步对传播模式进行监测,评估抗病毒或疫苗候选物,并阐明潜伏期变异性。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：2026年在一艘邮轮上出现的安第斯病毒(ANDV)近期病例引起了急诊临床医生的关注。 主要方向：本综述概述了汉坦病毒感染的流行病学、临床表现、诊断和管理,强调靶向内皮以及不同综合征(肾综合征出血热 vs 汉坦病毒肺综合征)。 研究现状：人类感染主要通过气溶胶化的啮齿动物排泄物传播,已建立诊断性ELISA检测,治疗以支持性治疗为主。 不足：近期安第斯病毒的人际传播证据凸显了传播动力学数据有限以及缺乏特异性抗病毒药物的现状。 后续研究：需要进一步对传播模式进行监测,评估抗病毒或疫苗候选物,并阐明潜伏期变异性。

papers.title: Omics Approaches in Hantavirus Research: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for two severe human diseases: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Worldwide case fatality rates vary from 1% to 40%. Although single-layer genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics studies have advanced our understanding of hantavirus biology, true multi-omics integration remains scarce, leaving systems-level mechanisms of disease severity and host-pathogen interactions unresolved. High-throughput omics technologies have greatly advanced the study of hantavirus-host interactions. This review summarizes genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and AI-enabled approaches in hantavirus research. Genomic studies have clarified viral diversity, evolution, and reassortment, while transcriptomics has identified regulatory networks governing endothelial and innate immune responses. Proteomics has revealed host proteins involved in immune regulation, endothelial dysfunction, and potential therapeutic targeting, whereas metabolomics indicates substantial metabolic reprogramming during infection, although dedicated studies remain limited. AI-based approaches are increasingly applied to outbreak prediction, surveillance, and risk modeling. Drawing on successful multi-omics frameworks developed for other viral infections, we discuss opportunities to improve biomarker discovery, surveillance, therapeutic development, and future precision medicine strategies for hantavirus infections.

source_records.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for two severe human diseases: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Worldwide case fatality rates vary from 1% to 40%. Although single-layer genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics studies have advanced our understanding of hantavirus biology, true multi-omics integration remains scarce, leaving systems-level mechanisms of disease severity and host-pathogen interactions unresolved. High-throughput omics technologies have greatly advanced the study of hantavirus-host interactions. This review summarizes genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and AI-enabled approaches in hantavirus research. Genomic studies have clarified viral diversity, evolution, and reassortment, while transcriptomics has identified regulatory networks governing endothelial and innate immune responses. Proteomics has revealed host proteins involved in immune regulation, endothelial dysfunction, and potential therapeutic targeting, whereas metabolomics indicates substantial metabolic reprogramming during infection, although dedicated studies remain limited. AI-based approaches are increasingly applied to outbreak prediction, surveillance, and risk modeling. Drawing on successful multi-omics frameworks developed for other viral infections, we discuss opportunities to improve biomarker discovery, surveillance, therapeutic development, and future precision medicine strategies for hantavirus infections.

papers.title: Andes virus and sin nombre virus: Similarities and distinctive features.
papers.abstract: The threat of hanta virus infection has come to the forefront in recent weeks, following the outbreak of the Andes virus aboard the Dutch-flagged MV Hondius cruise ship during its spring 2026 voyage. Several passengers and crew members got infected because Andes virus is the sole known hanta virus to trigger human-to-human infection. All exposed passengers have returned to their countries in Asia, the Americas and Europe, and remain in quarantine to this day because of Andes virus extended incubation period (35-45 days). Several infected patients have died due to Andes high mortality (35-50%). Taken together, the unfolding of these alarming facts has ignited fears of a new hanta virus pandemic. Here, we briefly outline certain among the major similarities and distinctive features between Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus, the two principal hanta viruses known today to infect humans. This writing emphasizes how timely and critical it is to develop concerted research and accelerated testing programs for anti-hanta virus vaccines and antivirals.
